channel.title: Atlas
channel.description: Rivers, lakes, mountains and deserts, and the lines we draw between them. A Day News demo feed.

item.title: The Danube flows through ten countries
item.description:
The Danube is Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga, running about 2,850 kilometers from the Black Forest in Germany to the Black Sea.

Along the way it passes through or along the borders of ten countries: Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine. No other river in the world touches so many.

Four capital cities stand on its banks: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.

item.title: Lake Baikal, the deepest lake on Earth
item.description:
Lake Baikal in southern Siberia is the world's deepest lake, reaching about 1,640 meters at its deepest point. It is also one of the oldest, formed in a rift valley some 25 million years ago.

Because it is so deep, Baikal holds more fresh water than any other lake: roughly a fifth of the unfrozen fresh water on Earth's surface, more than all of North America's Great Lakes combined.

In winter its surface freezes so clear in places that you can see through the ice to the stones below.

item.title: How tall is Mount Everest?
item.description:
In 2020, Nepal and China jointly announced a new official height for Mount Everest: 8,848.86 meters above sea level, the result of survey teams working from both sides of the mountain.

Measuring it is harder than it sounds. Surveyors have to work out where sea level would be beneath a mountain range, and decide whether to count the snow and ice on the summit. The 2020 figure measures to the top of the snow.

Everest is the highest mountain above sea level, but not the tallest from base to peak. Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises more than 10,000 meters from its base on the ocean floor.

item.title: The Atacama, where rain almost never falls
item.description:
The Atacama Desert, along the Pacific coast of northern Chile, is one of the driest places on Earth. Parts of it receive only a millimeter or two of rain a year, and some weather stations there have never recorded rain at all.

Its dry, clear air and high altitude make it one of the best places on the planet for astronomy, and several major observatories stand there.

Scientists also use its barren soils to test instruments bound for Mars, because few places on Earth are so similar.

item.title: Why the International Date Line zigzags
item.description:
The International Date Line runs roughly along the 180° meridian in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. Cross it heading west and the calendar jumps forward a day; heading east, it goes back one.

It is not a straight line. It bends around island groups so that neighboring islands can share a date. In 1995, Kiribati moved it far to the east so that the whole country, spread across more than 3,000 kilometers of ocean, would keep the same day.

No international treaty fixes the line. It simply follows the time zones that countries choose for themselves.

item.title: The Amazon carries more water than any other river
item.description:
The Amazon pours more water into the ocean than any other river: on average more than 200,000 cubic meters every second, around a fifth of all the river water that reaches the world's oceans.

That is more than the next several largest rivers combined, and the outflow is strong enough that its fresh water can be detected far out at sea.

Its basin covers about 7 million square kilometers of South America, much of it rainforest.
